title: jQuery and Legacy Code
summary: Read and maintain jQuery code: selecting and changing elements, events, Ajax, and how each maps to the modern DOM APIs you already know.
intro: jQuery is the most widely used JavaScript library ever written. In November 2026, a survey by W3Techs found it on about 63 percent of all websites, far more than any framework. WordPress, the software behind a large share of the web's sites, ships with it, and countless older apps, themes, and plugins are built on it. You won't start many new projects with jQuery, but you'll almost certainly work on one: fix a bug in a theme, add a feature to an old admin page, or take jQuery out of a site a piece at a time. The good news is that you already know what it does, since every jQuery method wraps a DOM API from the JavaScript lessons. This lesson shows why jQuery was built, how to read it, how its events and data fetching work, and how each piece maps to the code you'd write today.

steps.title: Why jQuery existed
steps.body:
jQuery code looks odd at first: dollar signs everywhere, and lines that chain one method after another. It all makes sense once you know what writing JavaScript for browsers was like in 2006, and why a library that hid the mess took over the web.

## The problem in 2006

Recall the frameworks lesson: browsers then did the same things in different ways. Internet Explorer had its own way to add event listeners and its own way to fetch data, and even reading an element's styles took different code in different browsers. There was no `querySelectorAll`, so finding every element with a class meant walking the page by hand. Every team wrote its own fixes, and each new browser version broke a few of them.

## jQuery's answer

John Resig released jQuery in 2006, with the slogan write less, do more. Its ideas:

- **Select with CSS.** `$(".menu li")` finds elements with the same selectors you'd write in a stylesheet, in every browser, years before browsers could do it themselves.
- **Act on the whole set.** A jQuery object holds every element the selector found, and a method like `.addClass("open")` changes all of them, with no loop.
- **Chain.** Most methods return the same object, so you can call the next one straight after: `$("#notice").text("Saved").addClass("ok").fadeIn()`.
- **Hide the differences.** Events, animation, and fetching data worked the same in every browser.
- **Plugins.** Anyone could add methods to jQuery objects, and thousands of plugins appeared: slideshows, date pickers, sortable tables, form checkers.

It worked so well that the standards caught up by copying it. `querySelectorAll`, `classList`, and `fetch` all do what jQuery did first.

## Why it's still everywhere

W3Techs, which surveys millions of sites, found jQuery on about 63 percent of all websites in November 2026, more than any other JavaScript library. WordPress, which runs a large part of the web, ships it and uses it on its own admin pages, so every theme and plugin can lean on it. Bootstrap needed it up to version 4, and many apps were built on it before React existed. Code that works doesn't get rewritten just because something newer came along.

## Versions

W3Techs also found that about four out of five sites with jQuery run version 3, and one in six still runs version 1. Version 3.7.1, from 2023, is what you'll meet most in code you maintain. In January 2026, version 4.0 removed functions that had been on their way out for years, like `$.trim`, `$.isArray`, and `$.parseJSON`, since `String.prototype.trim()`, `Array.isArray()`, and `JSON.parse()` do the same jobs, and it dropped support for Internet Explorer 10 and older. Version 4.1 is the current one, and 3.8, released next to it, is the last 3.x with anything new: from now on, 3.x only gets critical fixes. Everything this lesson teaches works the same in 3.x and 4.x.

## Adding it to a page

Like any library, jQuery comes from a CDN tag or from npm (example 1). The whole library is one function, named `jQuery`, with `$` as a short second name for it. To find out which version a page runs, ask that function in the console (example 2).

examples.title: Loading jQuery
examples.prompt: The end of a page's `<body>`, the way most jQuery sites load it. `trips.js` is the site's own code, which uses jQuery.
examples.explanation: The first tag loads jQuery 4.1.0 from code.jquery.com, jQuery's own CDN, with the `integrity` hash and `crossorigin` from the frameworks lesson. It's a classic script, so it defines `jQuery` and `$` as globals, names any later script can use. That's why order matters: `trips.js` has to come after it, or `$` won't exist yet when it runs. In a project with a build, you'd run `npm install jquery` and write `import $ from "jquery"` at the top of each module that uses it, and the bundler would handle the rest. In older code, expect the first form, often with an older version number in the file name.

examples.title: Which version is this page running?
examples.prompt: Paste this into the Console on a page that loads jQuery. `$.fn` is where jQuery keeps its methods, and `jquery` on it holds the version.
examples.explanation: This page loads jQuery 4.1.0, so that's what it prints. On a site you've just been handed, it's the first thing to check: the answer tells you which methods exist and which bugs to expect. If it prints a version that starts with 1, the site is on a version from 2016 or earlier, with known security holes, and that's worth raising. If the Console says `$` is not defined, the page doesn't use jQuery, or loads it under the name `jQuery` alone, which `jQuery.fn.jquery` would answer. A page that uses `$` for something else calls `jQuery.noConflict()`, which gives the `$` name back and keeps `jQuery`.

steps.title: Selecting and changing elements
steps.body:
Most jQuery code does two things: find elements, then change them. Every method stands for DOM code you already know, so reading jQuery is mostly seeing the DOM code underneath.

## $() and the jQuery object

`$("#tasks .task")` runs the selector and returns a **jQuery object**: a wrapper around every element it matched, numbered from 0 like an array, with a `length` (example 1). It's never `null`. When nothing matches, you get an empty set, and calling methods on it quietly does nothing. That's handy, and it's a trap: a typo in a selector raises no error, while `document.querySelector` returning `null` would have thrown one on the next line.

`$()` takes other things too. Give it a DOM element, as in `$(event.target)`, and it wraps that element. Give it a string of HTML, as in `$("<li>")`, and it makes a new element. Give it a function, and it runs the function once the page is ready (part 3). By habit, variables that hold jQuery objects start with `$`, like `$tasks`, so you can tell them from DOM elements at a glance.

```diagram jquery-set
One jQuery object wraps every matched element, and one call changes them all.
```

## Implicit iteration

Methods that change something apply to every element in the set, which jQuery calls **implicit iteration**. In the diagram, `$tasks.addClass("seen")` adds the class to all three tasks at once. Methods that read something are different: most read only the first element, so `$tasks.attr("class")` gives the first task's classes. `.text()` is the exception, and joins the text of all of them.

## Reading and changing

Most methods read when you give them no value, and set when you give them one: `.text()` reads the text and `.text("Done")` sets it.

- `.text()` and `.html()` are `textContent` and `innerHTML`. Part 4 shows why `.html()` with someone's input is dangerous.
- `.val()` is a form field's `value`.
- `.attr("href")` is `getAttribute`, and `.prop("checked")` reads the property, the split between attributes and properties from the JavaScript lessons. A checkbox's `checked` attribute says how it started, and its property says how it is now, so use `.prop()` for the live state.
- `.addClass()`, `.removeClass()`, `.toggleClass()`, and `.hasClass()` are `classList`.
- `.css("color", "red")` sets an inline style, and `.css("color")` reads the computed one.
- `.data("count")` reads a `data-count` attribute, and turns `"5"` into the number 5 and `"true"` into `true`, unlike `dataset`, which always gives strings.

## Moving around the page

- `.find(".price")` searches inside each element, like `querySelectorAll` on an element.
- `.closest("li")` walks up to the nearest ancestor that matches, like the DOM's `closest`.
- `.parent()`, `.children()`, `.siblings()`, `.next()`, and `.prev()` step to neighbors.
- `.eq(1)` picks one element from the set, still wrapped, and `.first()` and `.last()` pick the ends.

## Making elements

`$("<li>", { text: "Buy milk" })` makes a new element with its text and attributes set. `.append()` and `.prepend()` put things inside an element, at the end or the start, and `.appendTo()` is the same thing written the other way round, which chains nicely (example 2). `.remove()` takes elements off the page.

## Back to the DOM

A jQuery object isn't an element. `$tasks[0]`, or `$tasks.get(0)`, gives you the first DOM element inside it, for code or a library that needs a real one, and `$(element)` wraps one back up. Mixing the two is fine, as long as you know which one you're holding.

examples.title: A set of three tasks
examples.prompt: The page has a list with the id `tasks` and three items with the class `task`: Buy milk, Call the dentist, which also has the class `done`, and Read about bundlers. This runs in a script after jQuery.
examples.output:
3
Buy milkCall the dentistRead about bundlers
task
3
0
Buy milk
true
examples.explanation: The set holds three elements. `.text()` joins the text of all three, with nothing in between, while `.attr("class")` reads only the first, which has just `task`. `addClass` changed all three, so selecting `.seen` afterwards finds three. `#missing` matches nothing, so its set is empty, and calling `addClass` on it does nothing and throws nothing: if that had been a typo, you'd never hear about it. `$tasks[0]` is the plain DOM element for Buy milk, so `textContent` works on it. `.eq(1)` is the second task, still wrapped in jQuery, and it does have the class `done`.

examples.title: Making elements and chaining
examples.prompt: Replace whatever is in the list with the id `notes` with one item for each note.
examples.explanation: `.empty()` removes everything inside the list and returns the same set, so it chains straight into the variable. In the loop, `$("<li>", { ... })` makes a list item whose text is set with `textContent` underneath, so the note is never read as HTML, and whose `data-id` attribute is set too. `.addClass` and `.appendTo` chain onto it, each returning the new item. The last line counts the list's children, two, and reads the last note's `data-id` with `.data`, which turned the attribute's text into the number 2. Written with the DOM, the loop would be `createElement`, `textContent`, `dataset`, `classList.add`, and `append`.

steps.title: Events, effects, and Ajax
steps.body:
Pages respond to people, and jQuery's ways of handling events and fetching data show up in nearly every jQuery file. Their shapes differ a little from the DOM's, and a couple of those differences cause real bugs.

## Waiting for the page

`$(function () { ... })` runs the function once the HTML has been read and the DOM is built, like a listener for `DOMContentLoaded`. Older code writes it `$(document).ready(function () { ... })`, which does the same. It mattered when scripts sat in the head without `defer`. With `defer` or a module script, from the JavaScript lessons, the DOM is ready by the time your code runs, and the wrapper isn't needed.

## Events

`.on("click", handler)` is `addEventListener`, on every element in the set, and `.off("click", handler)` takes it off again. Inside the handler, `this` is the element the event is for, and `$(this)` wraps it, which is why jQuery code is full of `$(this)`. The handler gets an event object with the DOM's familiar parts: `event.target`, `event.preventDefault()`, and `event.stopPropagation()`.

Give `.on()` a selector as its second argument and it does the event delegation from the JavaScript lessons: one listener on a parent handles events from any child that matches, including children added later (example 1). Inside, `this` is the child that matched, not the parent.

Two habits in old code to watch for:

- Shortcut methods like `.click(handler)` and `.submit(handler)` do the same as `.on("click", handler)`. They've been **deprecated**, marked as on their way out, since version 3.3, and they still work.
- `return false` from a jQuery handler does both `preventDefault()` and `stopPropagation()`. Code that returns false to stop a link from opening also stops every listener further up from hearing the click, which breaks delegation somewhere else, and is a classic hard-to-find bug.

## Effects

`.hide()` and `.show()` set `display`. `.fadeIn()`, `.fadeOut()`, `.slideUp()`, `.slideDown()`, and `.animate()` change styles a little at a time with JavaScript timers, many times a second, on the main thread. Recall from the CSS lessons that a transition on `opacity` or `transform` runs smoothly even while JavaScript is busy, and that `prefers-reduced-motion` lets people ask for less movement. jQuery's effects ignore that setting unless you set `$.fx.off = true` yourself. In new code, toggle a class and let CSS do the animating.

## Ajax

**Ajax**, short for Asynchronous JavaScript and XML, is the old name for fetching data without reloading the page, from when the data was usually XML, an older text format that marks up data with tags, the way HTML marks up a page. jQuery's `$.ajax()` takes an object of settings, and `$.getJSON(url)` is the short form for fetching JSON. Both return a **jqXHR**, an object that is also a **Deferred**: jQuery's own kind of promise, from before promises were part of JavaScript. You attach `.done()` for success, `.fail()` for errors, and `.always()` for either (example 2).

Since version 3, a Deferred works with `await` and `.then()` like a real promise, so `const notes = await $.getJSON("/notes.json")` works. Two differences from `fetch` matter when you move code from one to the other:

- `$.ajax` treats an HTTP error as a failure, so a 404 lands in `.fail()`, or throws when you await it. `fetch` only rejects when the network fails, so you check `response.ok` yourself, as the fetch lesson showed.
- `$.ajax` sends its `data` as form fields, `name=value&...`, like the form posts from the forms lesson. To send JSON, you pass `JSON.stringify(data)` and `contentType: "application/json"` yourself.

examples.title: Delete buttons with one listener
examples.prompt: `trips.js` on an older admin page. Each task in the list with the id `tasks` has a delete button with the class `delete`, and tasks can be added after the page loads.
examples.explanation: The outer function waits for the DOM. The listener sits on the list itself, and the `".delete"` selector makes it a delegated one: a click anywhere in the list runs the handler only when it came from a delete button, including buttons on tasks added later. `this` is the button that was clicked, so `$(this).closest("li")` finds its task. `.fadeOut(200, ...)` fades the task over 200 ms with timers, then calls its function with `this` set to the faded element, which removes it. The DOM version is one `addEventListener` on the list that checks `event.target.closest(".delete")`, and a CSS transition for the fade.

examples.title: Fetching JSON, and what a 404 does
examples.prompt: Load notes from a file that exists, then from one that doesn't. `notes.json` holds an array of two notes.
examples.explanation: `$.getJSON` fetches the file and parses it as JSON, and `.done()` gets the result, the array. `.fail()` gets three things: the jqXHR, with the status code on it, a word for what went wrong, here `"error"`, and the status text. The second load waits in `.always()` until the first is finished, so they run in order. When we ran it against Python's server, it printed loaded 2 notes from /notes.json, then failed: 404 File not found for /missing.json, and the Console added a red line of its own for the failed request. With `fetch`, that 404 would have resolved, not failed, and `response.ok` would have been false.

steps.title: Reading and migrating jQuery
steps.body:
Sooner or later, you'll be asked to change some jQuery code, or to get rid of it. Both start with reading it as the DOM code it stands for, and this table does most of the translating.

## jQuery and the DOM, side by side

| jQuery | The DOM |
| --- | --- |
| `$(".task")` | `document.querySelectorAll(".task")` |
| `$(fn)` | a `defer` or module script, or `DOMContentLoaded` |
| `$el.on("click", fn)` | `el.addEventListener("click", fn)` |
| `$list.on("click", ".delete", fn)` | a listener on `list` that checks `event.target.closest(".delete")` |
| `$el.addClass("open")` | `el.classList.add("open")` |
| `$el.text("Saved")` | `el.textContent = "Saved"` |
| `$el.html(markup)` | `el.innerHTML = markup` |
| `$input.val()` | `input.value` |
| `$el.attr("href")` | `el.getAttribute("href")` |
| `$box.prop("checked")` | `box.checked` |
| `$el.data("id")` | `el.dataset.id`, always a string |
| `$el.find(".price")` | `el.querySelectorAll(".price")` |
| `$el.closest("li")` | `el.closest("li")` |
| `$("<li>", { text })` | `document.createElement("li")`, then `textContent` |
| `$list.append($item)` | `list.append(item)` |
| `$el.remove()` | `el.remove()` |
| `$el.hide()` | `el.hidden = true` |
| `$el.fadeIn()` | a class and a CSS transition |
| `$.getJSON(url)` | `fetch(url)`, check `response.ok`, then `response.json()` |
| `$.each(items, fn)` | `for (const item of items)` |

One thing doesn't fit in a row. A jQuery method acts on every element in its set, and a DOM method acts on one element, so `$(".task").addClass("seen")` becomes a loop over `document.querySelectorAll(".task")` that calls `classList.add("seen")` on each.

## Mixing old and new

jQuery and plain DOM code live together fine. They work on the same elements and the same events, so a listener added with `addEventListener` hears a real click just like one added with `.on()`. Two things trip people up. A jQuery object isn't an element, so pass `$el[0]` to code that wants one. And `.trigger("saved")` runs the jQuery handlers for a made-up event like `saved`, but a listener added with `addEventListener` never hears it.

## The XSS trap

Recall cross-site scripting from the JavaScript lessons: putting someone else's text into the page as HTML lets them run code in it. In jQuery, every method that accepts HTML does that: `.html()`, `.append()`, `.prepend()`, `.before()`, `.after()`, and `$()` itself, when its string looks like HTML. Old jQuery code builds markup by gluing strings together all the time, and every place where a user's name, comment, or search is glued in is a hole (example 1). Use `.text()`, or make the element and set its text, which keeps text as text. Versions before 3.5 also had flaws of their own in how they cleaned up HTML, which is one more reason to upgrade.

## Keep it, or move off it

There's no prize for removing jQuery from code that works, so weigh it:

- **Keep it and upgrade** when the site is stable and jQuery runs through everything. At least move to the latest 3.x for its fixes. To go to 4.x, add the **jQuery Migrate** plugin first: it puts back what 4.0 removed and prints a warning in the Console each time old code uses it, so you can fix them one at a time, then take the plugin out.
- **Move off it step by step** when you're working on the code anyway. Write new code with the DOM, and rewrite each old file in plain JavaScript when you touch it (example 2). When the last use is gone, delete the script tag, and every page is 28 kB lighter.
- **Check the plugins first.** jQuery often stays because of a plugin built on it, like a date picker, a slideshow, or a data table. Find a replacement for the plugin before planning the removal.
- **On WordPress, leave it.** WordPress loads jQuery itself, and many plugins expect it.

Most real projects end up doing the first two at once: they keep jQuery up to date to stay safe, and use less of it over time.

The next and last lesson turns to Tailwind, the CSS framework many new projects start with.

examples.title: A search title with a hole in it
examples.prompt: A search page shows what was searched for, taken from the `q` in its query string. The first line of jQuery is the kind of code you'll find, and the second is the fix.
examples.explanation: The first version glues the search into a string of HTML and hands it to `.html()`. Search for shoes and it's fine. Send someone a link whose `q` holds ``, and the browser builds that image, fails to load it, and runs the code in `onerror`, on your site, with your visitor's cookies. The second version never treats the search as HTML: `.text()` sets the plain words, and `$("")` makes an empty bold element whose text is then set with `.text(query)`, so any angle brackets show up as angle brackets. Search a jQuery project for `.html(`, `.append(`, and `$("<` with a `+` nearby, and check every one.

examples.title: The delete buttons without jQuery
examples.prompt: Example 1 from part 3, rewritten with the DOM, and now also telling the server. It's a module script, so the DOM is ready when it runs. `#error` is a paragraph with the `hidden` attribute.
examples.explanation: `$(function ...)` is gone, since a module runs after the DOM is built. The delegated `.on()` became one `addEventListener` on the list, plus `closest(".delete")` to find out whether the click came from a delete button, and to ignore it if not. `$(this).closest("li")` became `button.closest("li")`. The request uses `fetch` with the `DELETE` method, and because `fetch` doesn't fail on a 404 or a 500, `deleteTask` checks `response.ok` and throws, so a failed delete leaves the task in place and shows the message. The fade is gone too. If the design needs it, a class with a CSS transition brings it back, and it respects reduced motion for free.

recap:
- jQuery smoothed over browser differences in 2006, and still runs on most websites, WordPress included.
- $() returns a jQuery object: a set of elements that's never null, where setters change all and most getters read the first.
- .text, .html, .val, .attr, .prop, .addClass, .find, and .closest each stand for a DOM API you know.
- .on() with a selector delegates events, and return false stops both the default action and propagation.
- $.ajax returns a Deferred that works with await, and unlike fetch, it fails on a 404.
- .html(), .append(), and $() with glued-together strings are XSS holes, so set text with .text().
- Version 4 removed old helpers: upgrade with jQuery Migrate, or replace jQuery a file at a time.
